prompt: Which operation does Microsoft fix at exactly one request unit?
hint: The cheapest thing Cosmos DB does.

choices.text: A write of a 1 KB item
choices.why: A write costs more than a read of the same item.

choices.text: A point read of a 1 KB item
choices.why: Right: the point read is the anchor of the whole scale.

choices.text: A query that returns one 1 KB item
choices.why: A query has its own cost, and usually more than a point read of the same item.

choices.text: Any request of up to 1 KB, read or write
choices.why: Size is one factor among several; the kind of operation is another.

prompt: Which of these raise the request units of an operation? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of them changes nothing about the work.

choices.text: A larger item
choices.why: Right: more bytes to read, write and index.

choices.text: More indexed properties, on a write
choices.why: Right: every indexed property is work on every write.

choices.text: A query that does not name its partition key
choices.why: Right: it is sent to every physical partition.

choices.text: Running the same query a second time
choices.why: The charge is deterministic: the same operation on the same data costs the same.

prompt: Every answer from Cosmos DB says what the operation cost in the header `x-ms-request-___`.
hint: What the operation was billed.

prompt: `charges.py` reported 1 for a 9 KB write and for a query across partitions. What do you do with those numbers?
hint: What did the emulator say for everything else?

choices.text: Use them as a lower bound for the estimate
choices.why: They bound nothing: the emulator reports the same 1 for everything.

choices.text: Multiply them by the size in KB to get Azure's figure
choices.why: There is no published formula, and a placeholder times anything is still a placeholder.

choices.text: Nothing: measure the charges on a real account instead
choices.why: Right: the header is in the right place and holds a placeholder.

choices.text: Trust them for writes and not for queries
choices.why: Writes are just as flat: 1 KB and 9 KB both came back as 1.

prompt: Match each way of paying to what it bills.
hint: One description belongs to none of them.

pairs.right: Each hour's highest RU/s, never below a tenth of the maximum
The request units consumed, per million

right_distractors: The bytes returned to the client

prompt: An autoscale container has a maximum of 4,000 RU/s. What is the lowest level it is billed at in an hour, in RU/s?
hint: A tenth of the ceiling.

prompt: Autoscale costs 1.5 times manual per RU/s. Below what average share of its maximum must its hours be billed for it to be cheaper?
hint: Manual pays for the maximum every hour.

choices.text: One half
choices.why: At one half autoscale costs 0.75 of manual, but the break-even is higher.

choices.text: Two thirds
choices.why: Right: 1.5 times two thirds is one, the price of manual.

choices.text: One tenth
choices.why: A tenth is the floor it never goes below, not the break-even.

choices.text: Fifteen per cent
choices.why: That confuses the factor 1.5 with a share.

prompt: `modes.py` asked for a container at 100 RU/s and the emulator created it and reported 100. What would Azure have done?
hint: What is the manual minimum?

choices.text: Refused it: manual throughput starts at 400 RU/s
choices.why: Right, and the emulator also answered every container with the last one's offer.

choices.text: Created it at 100, since throughput moves in steps of 100
choices.why: The steps are of 100 above a minimum of 400.

choices.text: Created it as serverless, which has no minimum
choices.why: Serverless is chosen for the account, not given to a container that asked for too little.

choices.text: Created it with autoscale up to 1,000 RU/s
choices.why: Nothing converts a manual request into autoscale.

prompt: Why did autoscale cost less than a quarter of manual in `sizing.py`?
hint: Look at the last line it printed.

choices.text: Because autoscale has a lower price per RU/s
choices.why: It has a higher one, 1.5 times.

choices.text: Because autoscale ignores the promotion hour
choices.why: It bills that hour at 2,700, like manual does.

choices.text: Its hours averaged 14% of the maximum
choices.why: Right: one busy hour and twenty-three quiet ones.

choices.text: Because serverless set a ceiling on it
choices.why: The three are priced independently.

prompt: At the illustrative prices, below what share of the time, in per cent to the nearest whole number, must reserved capacity be busy for serverless to be cheaper than manual?
hint: 0.008 dollars for an hour of 100 RU/s against 360,000 units at 0.25 per million.

prompt: Quitanda's load becomes 300 orders a second around the clock. Which way of paying wins now, and why?
hint: What share of its maximum is autoscale billed at?

choices.text: Manual, by the same arithmetic
choices.why: Right: autoscale is billed at its maximum every hour at 1.5 times the price, 233.28 against 155.52.

choices.text: Autoscale, because it always follows the load
choices.why: There is nothing to follow: the load is flat at the peak.

choices.text: Serverless, because the units are consumed anyway
choices.why: Consumed units cost far more than reserved ones that are used: 1,749.60.

choices.text: They cost the same once the load is steady
choices.why: The price per unit still differs by 1.5 times.

prompt: Which numbers in `sizing.py` should be replaced first, before any price?
hint: They were called assumptions.

choices.text: The number of days in the month
choices.why: Thirty is arithmetic, not a guess about Cosmos DB.

choices.text: The request charges and the order counts
choices.why: Right: measure the first on an account and take the second from the shop's records.

choices.text: The rounding of every amount up to hundreds of RU/s
choices.why: That is how throughput is set and billed.

choices.text: The minimum of 400 RU/s
choices.why: That is documented, not assumed.

prompt: A request needs more request units than its second has left. What does Cosmos DB answer?
hint: Too many.

choices.text: It queues the request until the next second and answers 200
choices.why: Nothing is queued; the request is refused and the client waits.

choices.text: 429, with `x-ms-retry-after-ms`
choices.why: Right: nothing is written, and the header says how long to wait.

choices.text: 503, and the container scales up
choices.why: Manual throughput never changes itself.

choices.text: It serves it and bills the extra units at a higher rate
choices.why: There is no overdraft: the budget is per second.

prompt: A container is provisioned at 30,000 RU/s over three physical partitions. How many RU/s can every item with one partition key get at most?
hint: One key lives in one physical partition.

prompt: Normalized RU Consumption sits at 100% while the container uses a fifth of its throughput. What is the fix?
hint: Which partition is at 100%?

choices.text: Double the container's throughput
choices.why: The hot key stays in one partition; the others get more to leave idle.

choices.text: Raise the library's retry count
choices.why: More retries spend more units the partition does not have.

choices.text: Switch the container to serverless
choices.why: Serverless is chosen per account, and the one-key ceiling holds there too.

choices.text: A partition key that spreads the load
choices.why: Right: one partition at its budget and the rest idle is a hot partition.

prompt: `flood.py` wrote 2,000 orders to a 400 RU/s container in 12.8 seconds with no retries. What does that show?
hint: Who was asked?

choices.text: That 400 RU/s carries 156 writes a second
choices.why: At the illustrative 6 RU a write it carries about 66.

choices.text: Only how fast the program and the laptop are
choices.why: Right: the emulator never throttles.

choices.text: That the library absorbed the throttling
choices.why: It reported zero throttled attempts for every write.

choices.text: That writes are not counted against throughput
choices.why: They are, and cost more than reads.

prompt: Left at its defaults, how does the Python library 4.17.1 handle a 429?
hint: Ask the library, as the section did.

choices.text: It raises it at once, for the program to decide
choices.why: It retries first; the program hears only about the ones that outlast that.

choices.text: It retries forever, waiting one second each time
choices.why: There is a limit, and no fixed interval by default.

choices.text: 9 retries, 30 seconds, waits as asked
choices.why: Right: 9, 30 and no fixed interval, from `RetryOptions`.

choices.text: It retries 3 times within 5 seconds
choices.why: Those are the numbers `writer.py` chose, not the defaults.

prompt: Put in order what happens to a throttled write in `writer.py`, from the first answer.
hint: The program hears about it last.
items: The library waits the time the header asked for
The library sends the write again, up to three times
The retries or the five seconds run out

prompt: A third of a container's requests are throttled. Why is raising the retry count the wrong fix?
hint: What does a retry spend?

choices.text: Retries spend units too
choices.why: Right: the load grows and latency climbs; the fix is capacity, the key or less work.

choices.text: Because Azure caps retries at nine
choices.why: Nine is the library's default, and it is configurable.

choices.text: Because retries turn reads into writes
choices.why: A retried read is still a read.

choices.text: Because a retried request costs nothing and hides the problem
choices.why: It hides the problem, but it is charged like any other request.

prompt: Quitanda adds a container of delivery receipts, written once per order and read a few hundred times a day in total. Which way of paying, at the illustrative prices?
hint: How busy would 400 reserved RU/s be?

choices.text: Manual at 400 RU/s, the cheapest setting
choices.why: Reserved all day and busy far less than 9% of it.

choices.text: Autoscale up to 1,000 RU/s, since it scales down at night
choices.why: It never goes below 100 billed, still mostly idle.

choices.text: Serverless, on an account created for it
choices.why: Right: busy well under 9% of the time, and serverless is chosen for the whole account.

choices.text: Whichever the emulator reports as cheapest
choices.why: The emulator reports a placeholder charge and the wrong container's offer.

prompt: At an illustrative 6 RU a write, about how many writes a second does a 400 RU/s container carry? Round down.
hint: 400 divided by 6.

prompt: Which did the emulator do in this lesson that Azure would not? Choose all that apply.
hint: One is the library, not the emulator.

choices.text: Charge 1 for a write of 9 KB
choices.why: Right: a placeholder.

choices.text: Accept a container at 100 RU/s
choices.why: Right: the manual minimum is 400.

choices.text: Take 2,000 writes in 12.8 seconds at 400 RU/s without a 429
choices.why: Right: it never throttles.

choices.text: Retry a throttled request nine times by default
choices.why: That is the library's policy, and it would apply on Azure too.
